posts.title: Double Binds and Hegel's Who Thinks Abstractly?
posts.description: Hegel argues against 'abstract thinking.' Really, he makes the claim that his reader is already against abstract thinking and attempts to make the identity of the practitioners of it legible to the reader. Who thinks abstractly? The uneducated, not the educated. Good society does not think abstractly because it is too easy, because it is too lowly (not referring to the external status) — not from an empty affectation of nobility that would place itself above that of which it is not capable, but on account of the inward inferiority of the matter. Abstract thinking is done by the uneducated—the nobles are too good for it. What is abstract thinking? This is abstract thinking: to see nothing in the murderer except the abstract fact that he is a murderer, and to annul all other human essence in him with this simple quality. posts.title: Don't Give up on Liberalism Yet
posts.description: This memo was generated for a nascent political theory group, on 19 Feb 2026. Discussion on Google Docs is omitted. It was written in response to Logan Graves’ “Speaking of Liberalism and Post-liberalism,” his “Speaking of Liberalism and Post-liberalism (Addendum),” and my “Desiderata for a Futurist Political Plan.” This memo concerns itself with Landian critiques of liberalism, much more than Thielian or other critiques. The latter must be covered in a future memo. Don't Give up on Liberalism Yet Nothing human makes it out of the near future. — Nick Land, “Meltdown” Upon reading Logan’s “Speaking of Liberalism and Post-liberalism,” and its corresponding Addendum, I realized that I did not yet find myself convinced that liberalism is incorrect. So let us attempt to formulate a description of a liberal future, and find where it might break. First, what liberalism, and why liberalism.
